back: Forms when molten rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens, e.g. granite, basalt or pumice.
Forms when layers of sediment are compacted and cemented, e.g. sandstone, mudstone or limestone. It may contain fossils.
Existing rock changed by heat and pressure without melting, e.g. marble (from limestone), slate or schist.
Magma is molten rock underground. Lava is molten rock that has reached the surface.

front: What does crystal size tell you about an igneous rock?
back: Large crystals: it cooled slowly underground (granite). Small crystals: it cooled quickly at the surface (basalt).
Weathering and erosion → deposition → compaction and cementation (sedimentary) → heat and pressure (metamorphic) → melting → cooling (igneous) → uplift.
Earth's thin, solid outer layer: about 5–10 km thick under the oceans and 30–50 km under the continents.
A thick layer (about 2900 km) of very hot rock that is mostly solid but flows very slowly.
Iron and nickel. The outer core is liquid; the inner core is solid because of the huge pressure.
A huge slab of crust and upper mantle that moves slowly (a few cm per year), driven partly by convection currents in the mantle.

front: Which plates meet under New Zealand?
back: The Pacific Plate and the Australian Plate.
One plate sliding down beneath another. Under the North Island, the Pacific Plate subducts beneath the Australian Plate.
A plate boundary running about 600 km along the South Island, where the plates slide past each other and push up the Southern Alps. The last big earthquake was in 1717.
An area of volcanoes and geothermal activity from Ruapehu to Whakaari/White Island, caused by subduction under the North Island.
Stress builds up in rocks along a fault until they suddenly slip, sending out shaking waves.
Breaking rock into smaller pieces where it is, e.g. by freeze–thaw, plant roots or acidic rain.
Moving weathered rock away, by rivers, waves, wind, glaciers or gravity.
Weathered rock particles (sand, silt, clay), humus, water, air and living things.
The preserved remains or traces of a living thing from long ago, usually found in sedimentary rock.

front: In undisturbed rock layers, which layer is oldest?
back: The bottom layer, because each layer settles on top of the one before.
